report:
**Conclusion:** The health claim that conjugated linoleic acid (CLA) supplements effectively reduce abdominal fat is **unsupported** by high-quality scientific evidence. 

Although early rodent studies demonstrated significant fat loss, human clinical trials and systematic meta-analyses show that CLA's effects in humans are minor, inconsistent, and clinically insignificant:

* **Minimal Overall Fat Loss:** Systematic reviews of randomized clinical trials (RCTs) show that CLA supplementation produces only a small reduction in overall fat mass (approximately 0.05 kg or 0.1 lbs per week).
* **No Targeted Abdominal Reduction:** High-quality clinical trials demonstrate that CLA does not specifically target abdominal or visceral fat, nor does it meaningfully decrease waist circumference compared to placebos.
* **Lack of Clinical Relevance:** Comprehensive meta-analyses published in nutrition journals conclude that any observed body composition changes are too small to yield clinically meaningful weight-loss or health benefits.

In summary, CLA supplements are not an effective solution for spot-reducing abdominal fat.

**Sources:**
* *British Journal of Nutrition Meta-Analysis:* https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366
* *The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition Meta-Analysis:* https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext
* *European Journal of Nutrition Systematic Review:* https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-011-0253-9
* *PubMed Central (PMC) Clinical Overview:* https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4429457/
